newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian economy quakes as pyramids tumble.
newsitem.headline: Albanian economy quakes as pyramids tumble.

text.p: Albania, Europe's poorest country, is likely to become poorer still following the collapse of immensely popular pyramid investment schemes, analysts said on Wednesday.
The schemes hurt the economy while they were thriving, voraciously sucking up cash which would have been better spent trying to create new businesses in the small Balkan state.

But the recent failure of many of the high-yielding funds, which economists believe have tied up as much as $1.5 billion, could inflict far greater damage on a country which has only recently broken free from the chains of hardline communism.

"There are many risks including hyper inflation, a fall in foreign investment and a dramatic drop in the local economy," said a foreign banking source, who declined to be named. "Not to mention the risk of more rioting," he added.

Thousands of Albanians, some of whom sold all their possessions to invest in the funds, went on the rampage last weekend when the extent of the collapse of the much-loved pyramid schemes became obvious.
The funds took off after the old communist regime was ousted in 1990, offering investors astonishing rates of return.

Lacking an efficient banking system, people entrusted their cash to the get-rich-quick funds, which prosper by paying investors with the deposits of the new and collapse when they run short of new investors.
Some Albanians sold everything they had to raise money for the schemes and enjoyed a life of idle luxury, living off the interest income.

"The damage done by the schemes was caused because the money was not put into productive growth. It also negatively affected the work ethic of some of the population," said Carlos Elbirt, the World Bank's resident representative in Tirana.
By the end of 1996, almost all Albania's 3.4 million people were somehow involved in the pyramids. The system reached saturation point and inevitably started to shrivel.
Five big funds have had their bank assets frozen or else declared bankruptcy.
In a bid to calm tension, the government promised to honour some of the debts, but economists say this may torch inflation, which is already running at 17.4 percent year-on-year.
"Where is the money going to come from to pay back these people?" Elbirt told Reuters. "There is not the money in the state budget and printing money would mean hyper inflation."

The impact of the failing funds is already being felt, with the Albanian lek losing almost 10 percent of its value against the dollar on the official market since the start of the year as people switch to hard currencies.
Banking sources said some state banks imposed limits on the amount of lek selling they would accept on Wednesday.
The falling lek spells danger for retail trade, with almost all consumer goods imported, especially from Italy and Greece.
The owner of a furniture store in central Tirana said he had not yet put up prices, but said that since the collapse of the pyramid system he had seen an 80 percent fall in custom.
A barman in the capital said his trade was down 50 percent. "Before people would spend their days in here using their interest money, but that's all gone now," he said.

The collapse of the funds came at a bad time for Albania's economy, whose annual gross domestic product is worth a little under $2.5 billion and which is still getting over the lifting of a United Nations trade blockade against neighbouring Serbia.
Zef Preci, director of the independent Albania Centre for Economic Research, estimates that illegal petrol exports to Serbia accounted for 10-15 percent of GDP between 1993-95.
Another vital flow of funds into Albania comes from its army of largely illegal immigrants. Officials say between $350-450 million was sent home by Albanians abroad in 1995.

"The biggest risk is that flows from immigrants might cease once they realise that their relatives have thrown their money away into these pyramids," an international banking source in Tirana said, declining to be named.
On the flip side, Preci said the financial crisis might persuade more people to flee abroad in search of wealth.
"One positive factor for the Albanian economy is that it will encourage a fresh wave of illegal immigration which will eventually help finances back home," he said.
